conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s 10 gentle questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything from normal new-mom “blues” to signs that might need extra support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. We’ll go one question at a own pace; you can pause or re-word anything you need. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty impossible?

Honestly, laughing feels kind of hard right now. I can still smile when my husband does something silly, but it doesn’t come easily—most things just feel flat or tiring. I’d say I’ve laughed maybe once or twice, and even then it faded quickly.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh a little, but it’s not like before. Most of the time it feels like I’m too tired or just not in the mood, so the funny side of things doesn’t really land.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get excited about small stuff—like when Grandma’s coming over so I can take a shower without rushing—but the big “can’t-wait” feeling is mostly gone. Things I used to love planning, like coffee with friends or even online shopping for the baby, feel more like chores I have to push myself through.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like, if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m just not doing it right or I missed something I should’ve known. It’s not constant, but a couple of times this week I’ve had that little voice saying I should be better at this mom thing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do feel anxious out of nowhere—like my heart races while I’m just sitting on the couch. Mostly it’s about the baby: is he breathing okay, am I burping him right, stuff like that. Even when everything looks fine, I can’t always shake the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, a few times I’ve suddenly felt this rush of fear, like something bad’s about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. It passes pretty quick, but it’s unsettling—like I’m bracing for trouble that isn’t there.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m treading water. The baby, the dishes, the laundry—it all piles up, and by late afternoon I’m running on empty. I manage, but it’s that constant “what’s next?” pressure, like I can never quite catch my breath.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy—more just tense and wired. Most nights it takes me a long time to drift off because my mind keeps circling around the baby’s breathing, did I sterilize the bottles right, stuff like that. Once I’m asleep I’m usually OK, but getting there is hard several nights a week.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—not all day, but it hits in waves, especially when I’m alone with the baby and everything feels quiet and heavy. It’s not hopeless, just a low, tired kind of miserable that lingers for a bit and then lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I’ve teared up once or twice—like when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch—but actual crying has been rare this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I would never want to hurt myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**

**Presenting symptoms**  
- Anhedonia: reduced capacity to laugh/enjoy activities  
- Low mood with “waves” of sadness, especially when alone  
- Excessive self-blame regarding infant care (“should be better at this mom thing”)  
- Persistent, intrusive worries about infant safety; episodic panic sensations  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to ruminative worry  
- Daily sense of being overwhelmed/treading water  

**Pattern**  
Responses consistently reflect mild–moderate depressive features (loss of pleasure, sadness) superimposed on prominent postpartum anxiety (spontaneous panic, safety checking, racing thoughts at bedtime). No anhedonia is absolute, and no self-harm ideation reported.  

**Screening significance**  
- Positive indicators for postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety  
- Functional impact evident (fatigue, difficulty completing tasks, bedtime distress)  
- Absence of suicidal ideation or intent lowers acute safety risk  

**Risk factors noted**  
✓ Depressed mood with anhedonia  
✓ Sleep disruption secondary to worry  
✓ Excessive guilt/self-criticism  
✓ Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety/panic symptoms  
✓ Subjective sense of inadequate coping  

**Clinical impression (screening only)**  
Findings are above threshold for routine postpartum mood/anxiety follow-up; recommend standardized assessment (EPDS, GAD-7) and discussion of support/psychotherapeutic options.
